rules.statement: Model a vocabulary that may grow as `public const string` names in a static class, compared ordinally and documented as the known values, so consumers and sibling packages extend it by registering instead of editing the library.
rules.why: Every vocabulary is open by default. An enum fixes its members at compile time and closes the extension point to any package that didn't exist when it was written.
rules.check: Look for a new `enum` or closed type that models names, kinds, scopes, reasons, formats or methods that another package could plausibly add. Also look for string-name comparisons that don't use `StringComparison.Ordinal` or `StringComparer.Ordinal`.

rules.statement: Introduce an `enum` only when all three conditions hold: its members are fixed by something that can't grow without this library changing (a finite enumeration of an external specification the library implements in full, the outcome set of a library-owned operation, or a mirror of a framework type); no package other than this one could ever need another member; and a new member would require a change to this library anyway.
rules.why: Closing a vocabulary is the exception, and a reviewer must be able to justify it in three sentences. Asking 'does this package own today's members?' led to designs that shut out extensions.
rules.check: For each new or changed `enum`, try to state the three-part justification. Flag the enum if a package other than this one could ever need to add a member, or if a member is being added for another package's sake.

rules.statement: Don't ask to replace an enum with string names when it passes the three-part test, for example when it mirrors a finite registry or set of parameters defined by an RFC, mirrors a framework type, lists the options of a library-owned converter, or is the outcome set of one library-owned operation.
rules.why: A genuinely closed set gains exhaustiveness checking and type safety from an enum. Modeling it as strings would add validation with no extensibility to show for it.
rules.check: Before reporting an enum as a closed vocabulary, check whether its members come from a specification the library implements in full, from a framework type, or from the results of a single operation the library owns.

rules.statement: Don't put `[Flags]` on a vocabulary that may grow, and don't encode its hierarchy, compatibility or order in a `switch`, bit mask or hard-coded chain. Derive those relationships from registered data through a catalog.
rules.why: A `[Flags]` enum fixes the bit space and the meaning of every combination. Hard-coded relationships close the topology even when the names themselves are strings.
rules.check: Look for `[Flags]` enums, masks or `switch` statements that encode a cascade, parent/child order or compatibility among a vocabulary's members.

rules.statement: Don't choose behavior with an exhaustive `switch` over a vocabulary's members. Register each member's behavior as a strategy (through a DI strategy collection or `ICollectionDataSource<T>`) and dispatch to the registered strategy by name.
rules.why: A `switch` that grows with each extension closes the behavior to packages that can't edit it, which the ADR names as a smell that the wrong rule was chosen.
rules.check: Look for `switch` statements or expressions, or if/else chains, over vocabulary names or enum members that select an implementation, especially ones that would need a new case for each extension.

rules.statement: When a vocabulary's members carry registered data or strategies, resolve them through a catalog that validates the whole set when it is composed, rejecting duplicate names, dangling references and cycles.
rules.why: Open registration needs validation of the composed set so that a misregistration fails at composition rather than at use.
rules.check: Look at new catalogs or registries of named descriptors or strategies: check that composing them detects duplicate names, references to unregistered members and cyclic relationships.

rules.statement: Reject input that names an unregistered member of a vocabulary instead of ignoring it or falling back to a default.
rules.why: An open vocabulary is still closed to unregistered input. A name nobody registered must fail loudly.
rules.check: Look for lookups by name that silently skip unknown names, return a default, or continue when nothing is registered under the name.

rules.statement: Persist and transmit a vocabulary member as its name, never as an enum ordinal or numeric value.
rules.why: A node that meets an unknown member should fail closed by name instead of misreading a number.
rules.check: Look for enums stored as integers in persistence mappings or serialized as numbers in JSON or other wire formats (for example, a missing string enum converter or a cast to int).

rules.statement: Don't default to typed name wrappers (such as `readonly record struct Scope(string Name)`) for an open vocabulary. Use `const string` names, and reserve a wrapper for a signature that would otherwise confuse two name parameters.
rules.why: Wrappers add a type per vocabulary without adding openness. The family's open vocabularies are `const string` names.
rules.check: Look for new wrapper structs or records around a single name string that are introduced for a vocabulary without the motivation of disambiguating parameters.
